title: The doer's hat and auxiliary verbs
goal: Use the doer ending -k, master the auxiliaries dut/duzu/du, and build sentences about habits with the -t(z)en form.
bekal: put the "doer's hat" *-k* on the person who does something to something else
use *dut, duzu, du, dugu, duzue, dute* and their plural forms *ditut, dituzu, ditu*
build sentences about habits: *kafea edaten dut*, *euskara ikasten dut*

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Gosaria pisuan
dialogs.intro: Morning in the apartment. Unai, Budi's flatmate, is making breakfast.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.id: Good morning! What have you got in your hand?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Euskarazko liburu bat dut. Egunero irakurtzen dut.
lines.id: A book in Basque. I read it every day.
lines.literal: Basque-in-of book one I-have-it. every-day reading I-have-it.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Nik ere liburu hori dut! Non erosi duzu?
lines.id: I've got that book too! Where did you buy it?
lines.literal: I-doer also book that I-have-it! where bought you-have-it?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I bought it at the euskaltegi, for fifteen euros.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Merkea! Nik euskara ikasten dut, baina poliki.
lines.id: That's cheap! I'm learning euskara too, but slowly.
lines.literal: cheap-the! I-doer Basque learning I-have-it, but slowly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What do you do in the mornings?

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Kafea hartzen dut eta egunkaria irakurtzen dut.
lines.id: I have a coffee and read the paper.
lines.literal: coffee-the taking I-have-it and newspaper-the reading I-have-it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nik tea edaten dut. Ez dut kaferik edaten.
lines.id: I drink tea. I don't drink coffee.
lines.literal: I-doer tea-the drinking I-have-it. not I-have-it coffee-any drinking.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.text: Tea?! Euskaldunek kafea edaten dute beti!
lines.literal: tea?! Basque-person(pl)-doer coffee-the drinking they-have-it always!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Badakit, baina nik tea nahiago dut.
lines.id: I know, but I prefer tea.
lines.literal: yes-I-know-it, but I-doer tea-the want-more I-have-it.

notes: **Nik, not ni.** As soon as the sentence has something the action is done to — a book being read, coffee being drunk — the doer wears the *-k* hat. *Ni Budi naiz* (no hat, nothing being acted on) but *Nik liburua dut* (there's a book, so: hat on). This is the one truly new idea in the language, and this whole unit is about it.

**One auxiliary holds two pieces of information.** *Dut* isn't just "have": inside it are "I" (the doer) and "it" (a single thing being acted on). That's why the literal translation is `I-have-it`. If the thing is plural, the auxiliary changes: *ditut* = `I-have-them`.

**Egunero irakurtzen dut — a habit, not something happening now.** The *-t(z)en* form expresses what you usually do, just like the English present simple. For "I'm reading right now" you use *irakurtzen ari naiz*, covered in Unit 10.

**Ez dut kaferik edaten.** Notice three things at once: *ez* in front, the auxiliary jumping after it, and the verb thrown to the back. On top of that, *kafea* becomes *kaferik* — in a negative sentence, the thing acted on takes *-rik*, not *-a*.

blocks.text: This is the idea Basque is famous for. English marks the *subject* by putting it first. Basque doesn't care about the subject; it marks **the doer who does something to something else** with the ending *-k*.

So the question isn't "who's the subject?" but "is something being acted on?". If so, the doer wears the hat. If not, it stays bare. Basque even has a special question word for a doer with a hat: **nork?** (who does it), as opposed to **nor?** (who).

blocks.title: The most common trap: -ak and -ak
items: *Irakasleak* can mean two things: **"the teachers"** (plural, no hat) or **"the teacher, as doer"** (singular, with hat). The forms just happen to be the same.
The auxiliary tells them apart. *Irakasleak etorri **dira*** = the teachers have come (plural). *Irakasleak liburua irakurtzen **du*** = the teacher reads the book (singular, with hat).
The plural with a hat is different: *irakasle**ek***. Note the *e*: *euskaldun**ek** kafea edaten dute*.
Don't panic. Native speakers rely on the auxiliary to sort this out too, and the auxiliary is always there at the end of the sentence.

sections.title: The NORK-NOR auxiliary: the dut family

blocks.text: The auxiliary used with a doer wearing the hat is called *ukan*. On its own it means "to have", and it's the auxiliary for every verb that has an object. Learn both rows — it's the biggest investment in the whole course, and it pays off in every unit after this one.
Read the table as sentences, not as a list: *dut* = "I-have-it", *dituzte* = "they-have-them". The ending marks the doer; the middle marks how many things there are.

blocks.title: Why the verb moves in a negative
items: Positive sentence: `thing + verb + auxiliary` — *kafea edaten dut*.
Negative sentence: `ez + auxiliary + thing + verb` — *ez dut kaferik edaten*.
The auxiliary always sticks to *ez*, and since the auxiliary used to be at the end, the whole sentence swings around. It feels odd for the first two weeks, then becomes automatic.
Shortcut for beginners: learn *ez dut*, *ez duzu*, *ez du* as single chunks of sound, then add the rest after them.

blocks.text: To talk about what you usually do, the verb takes its *-t(z)en* form, followed by the auxiliary. The *-t(z)en* form is made from the dictionary form in three patterns.

The choice between *-tzen* and *-ten* follows the sound, not a neat rule — learn it word by word, like English irregular verbs. Luckily, the verbs you'll really use number fewer than forty, and they're all in the list at the end of the course.

blocks.title: Time words that go with habits
items: *egunero* (every day), *astero* (every week), *hilero* (every month), *urtero* (every year) — all made with the ending *-ero*.
They can go anywhere, but most often at the start of the sentence: *Normalean kafea hartzen dut.*

exercises.prompt: Put on the doer's hat if it's needed. If not, write the word as it is.
Fill in the blanks with the right auxiliary (dut, duzu, du, dugu, duzue, dute, ditut, ditu).
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Ni — Nik — Jonek — Jon — Haiek — Ikasleak
dut — duzu — du — ditugu — dute — ditut
Ez dut kaferik edaten. — Ez du egunkaririk irakurtzen. — Ez dugu euskararik ikasten. — Ez dute telebistarik ikusten. — Ez duzu ogirik jaten. — Ez dut libururik.
Nik euskara ikasten dut. — Unaik kafea edaten du. — Zer egiten duzu goizean? — Guk pintxoak jaten ditugu. — Ez dut egunkaririk irakurtzen. — Euskaldunek beti kafea edaten dute.
